name: Chest fly
pattern: Horizontal hug: arms stay almost straight and swing out wide and back together in front of the chest.
setup: Lie on the bench, dumbbells above your chest, palms facing each other.
Soft bend in the elbows, about 15-25°, and keep it fixed.
Shoulder blades back and down, feet planted.

steps.text: Lower the weights out to the sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch across the chest.
Stop with the elbows about level with the bench, not below it.
Bring the weights back up and together, as if hugging a tree.

cues.cue: Small fixed bend, do not turn it into a press.
cues.why: The fly loads the pecs at long lengths with the elbows almost straight; bending them shifts the work to the triceps.

cues.cue: Stop with elbows at bench level.
cues.why: Pec major tears are reported in flies; going below the torso stretches the tendon under load.

cues.cue: Keep them pinned back and down.
cues.why: It keeps the stretch in the chest instead of the front of the shoulder.

cues.cue: Use about half of your dumbbell press weight.
cues.why: Flies give similar peak pec activity to presses but for a shorter part of the rep, and need control.

breathing: Breathe in as the arms open, out as you bring them together.

tempo.note: Slow and even, short pause in the stretch.

mistakes.name: Turns into a press
mistakes.looks: Elbows bend a lot at the bottom and the weights come down near the chest.
mistakes.fix: Lock the slight elbow bend, use a lighter weight.
mistakes.why: The triceps take over and the chest loses its stretch.

mistakes.name: Arms drop too low
mistakes.looks: Elbows sink well below the bench and the shoulders roll forward.
mistakes.why: Large shoulder extension under load stresses the pec tendon and front shoulder.

mistakes.name: Shoulders come off the bench
mistakes.looks: At the top the shoulders round forward and lift.
mistakes.fix: Keep the blades pinned; hands meet over the chest, not past it.
mistakes.why: The shoulder blade leaves its stable position and the front delt takes over.

safety: Shoulder pain: shorten the range and use a machine or cables.
Never go heavy to failure in the bottom stretch without a spotter.

variants.change: Bench at about 30°: more upper chest.
Machine: peak pec activity about the same as the bench press (98%); fixed path.
Cables keep tension at the end where hands meet; bent-forward crossovers give about 93% of bench press pec activity.
Low-to-high: more upper chest. High-to-low: more lower chest.
One arm: brace the trunk against twisting.

subtypes.name: Pec deck / seated machine fly
subtypes.change: Seated upright, back on the pad, arms at shoulder height.

subtypes.name: Standing cable crossover
subtypes.change: Standing in a split stance between two pulleys, leaning slightly forward; hands meet low in front.

subtypes.name: Floor fly
subtypes.change: Lying on the floor: the elbows stop on the floor, so the stretch is short and safer.

subtypes.name: Svend and squeeze press
subtypes.change: Press a plate or two dumbbells together in front of the chest, squeezing the hands inward the whole time; elbows bend and straighten like a press.

subtypes.name: Suspension or ring fly
subtypes.change: Body leans like a push-up while the arms open and close; harder the lower you lean.

motion.basis: Coaching convention plus EMG (welsch2005, solstad2020, schanke2012); no kinematic study of the fly was found. All joint angles are estimates: elbows held at 15-25° and the upper arm reaching about bench level at the stretch; slight shoulder external rotation (palms up, elbows pointing down) at the stretch is estimated; scapula held retracted.

sources.cite: Solstad TEJ, Andersen V, Shaw M, Hoel EM, Vonheim A, Saeterbakken AH. A comparison of muscle activation between barbell bench press and dumbbell flyes in resistance-trained males. J Sports Sci Med. 2020;19(4):645-651.
Welsch EA, Bird M, Mayhew JL. Electromyographic activity of the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid muscles during three upper-body lifts. J Strength Cond Res. 2005;19(2):449-452.

Schanke W. Electromyographical analysis of the pectoralis major muscle during various chest exercises (Master's thesis, advisor Porcari J). University of Wisconsin-La Crosse; 2012. Commissioned by the American Council on Exercise.
Kolber MJ, Beekhuizen KS, Cheng MS, Hellman MA. Shoulder injuries attributed to resistance training: a brief review. J Strength Cond Res. 2010;24(6):1696-1704.
